**FDATA proposes framework to govern write access in open finance**

*The trade body's new policy paper categorises open finance activities into read, instruct and transact tiers, aiming to give North American regulators a structure for handling agentic AI and payment initiation as the sector moves beyond data-sharing.*

The Financial Data and Technology Association (FDATA) has published a policy framework designed to guide regulators in the US and Canada as open finance expands from read-only data access into write access, where third parties can initiate transactions on a consumer's behalf. The framework introduces three tiers of activity — read, instruct and transact — each with escalating requirements for consumer protection, authentication and liability.

Steve Boms, FDATA's executive director, said the framework is intended to give policymakers a principles-led approach rather than prescriptive rules, accommodating emerging use cases such as agentic fintech — where AI agents act autonomously on behalf of consumers. The paper argues that without a clear regulatory structure for write access, the industry risks either fragmented national approaches or a regulatory vacuum that could undermine consumer trust.

Several parallel regulatory processes make the framework's read-instruct-transact taxonomy relevant beyond North America. The FCA's AI sandbox is actively testing agentic applications, the HM Treasury consultation on payments regulation proposes a statutory right for variable recurring payments, and the ECB's digital euro work raises questions about how third-party access will function alongside a central bank digital currency. FDATA's framework is designed to provide a conceptual scaffold that could inform comparable debates in all three areas.

*Sources: [FDATA calls for a principles-led framework for the next generation of Open Finance](https://www.openbankingexpo.com/news/fdata-calls-for-a-principles-led-framework-for-the-next-generation-of-open-finance/) — Openbankingexpo | [FDATA Proposes New Policy Framework for Agentic Fintech and Write Access](https://ffnews.com/news/fdata-proposes-new-policy-framework-for-agentic-fintech-and-write-access) — Ffnews*

**Viva.com adds Wero wallet as EPI extends merchant reach**

*Viva.com has joined EPI and integrated Wero wallet payments into its platform, giving the scheme access to an acquirer network spanning 29 European markets beyond its core Franco-German banking base.*

Viva.com, the pan-European merchant acquirer, has joined the European Payments Initiative (EPI) and integrated Wero wallet payments into its platform. The move gives Wero access to Viva.com's merchant network across 29 European markets, offering a distribution channel that extends well beyond the scheme's existing footprint in France, Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria.

Since EPI's founding in 2020, its central difficulty has been less about technology than about achieving the network effects needed to compete with Visa, Mastercard and domestic schemes. Acquirer adoption is a critical step: merchants will not offer Wero at checkout without processor support, and consumers will not adopt it without merchant acceptance. Viva.com's participation addresses one side of that equation, though the scheme still faces the harder task of driving consumer demand in markets where card habits are entrenched.

The announcement follows Rabobank's decision in June 2025 to begin migrating iDEAL transactions to Wero in the Netherlands, and BoursoBank's integration of Wero for peer-to-peer payments in France. EPI remains in its early scaling phase, but the acquirer side of the network is filling in faster than the consumer side.

*Sources: [Viva.com adds Wero wallet after joining European Payments Initiative](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/currencies/articles/viva-com-adds-wero-wallet-074624419.html) — Yahoo Finance*

**US judge allows New York fraud lawsuit against Zelle to proceed**

*A federal judge has denied Zelle operator Early Warning Services' motion to dismiss New York's fraud lawsuit, keeping alive a case that could set expectations for real-time payment operators' liability for fraud losses.*

A US judge has rejected a motion by Early Warning Services, the bank consortium behind Zelle, to dismiss a lawsuit brought by New York attorney general Letitia James. The suit alleges Zelle failed to protect users from widespread fraud on its peer-to-peer payments network, and that participating banks did not adequately reimburse victims.

The ruling allows the case to proceed to discovery and potentially trial, keeping pressure on the operator of America's largest real-time peer-to-peer payment system. The core legal question — whether payment network operators bear responsibility for fraud that flows through their rails — has direct parallels to debates in the UK, where the PSR's mandatory APP fraud reimbursement regime has already shifted liability onto sending banks and payment firms.

The case tests a different model of accountability from the one emerging in Europe. The UK approach relies on regulation; this case could establish liability through litigation. Either route shapes the commercial calculus for any firm operating instant payment infrastructure, particularly as SEPA instant payments scale and verification of payee remains unevenly implemented.

*Sources: [Judge rejects Zelle bid to dismiss lawsuit over fraud losses](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48139/judge-rejects-zelle-bid-to-dismiss-lawsuit-over-fraud-losses?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra*

**Open finance could pose existential threat to advice sector, fintech commentator warns**

*Financial advisers risk disintermediation if they fail to engage with open finance data-sharing, according to Ian McKenna of the Financial Technology Research Centre, as the Financial Conduct Authority's (FCA) regulatory framework for the sector takes shape.*

Ian McKenna, founder of the Financial Technology Research Centre, has warned that open finance could represent an "existential threat" to the financial advice market if advisers do not adapt to a world where consumers can share portfolio, pension and banking data directly with competing services. The argument is that automated, data-driven tools could replicate much of what advisers currently do, particularly for mass-market clients, at a fraction of the cost.

The warning comes as the FCA develops its open finance regulatory framework, with pensions and investment data explicitly in scope following its roadmap. In Switzerland, industry-led initiatives have begun enabling the sharing of pension data between providers, though these are voluntary rather than regulatory mandates. The UK appears to be moving toward a more structured approach. For advisory firms, the risk is not that open finance will eliminate advice, but that it will compress margins on routine services and redirect client relationships toward platforms that can aggregate and act on data more efficiently.

The underlying dynamic is real: once consumers can consent to share financial data across providers, the switching costs that sustain advisory relationships fall sharply.

*Sources: [Open finance could pose 'existential threat' to advice market](https://www.professionaladviser.com/news/4533114/open-finance-pose-existential-threat-advice-market) — Professional Adviser*
